name: DraftKings Predictions (GUS III LLC d/b/a DraftKings Predictions; exchange arm rebranded DKeX, built on acquired Railbird Exchange)
positioning: "Sportsbook brand wearing a CFTC wrapper." Launched Dec 19, 2025 as a standalone iOS/Android/web app in 38 states (including CA, TX, FL, GA — states without legal online sports betting), explicitly positioned to reach customers DraftKings' sportsbook licenses can't. Structure at launch: DraftKings Predictions is a CFTC-registered Introducing Broker and NFA member that routes orders to third-party designated contract markets (CME Group at launch), with customer funds custodied at Wedbush Securities (per ValueTheMarkets). Strategic arc matters: Oct 21, 2025 it acquired Railbird (a CFTC-licensed DCM); May 22, 2026 Railbird d/b/a "DKeX" self-certified six sports contract templates (GAMEWIN, GAMESPREAD, game/player props, head-to-heads); June 26, 2026 DKeX launched as DraftKings' own exchange — integrated into the unified "DraftKings: Sports and Casino" app with live in-play contracts, eliminating per-trade fees paid to third-party exchanges. Claimed ~$11.3B annualized total trading volume ($3.4B consumer) for week ending June 21, 2026. Positioning is deliberately NOT financial-markets-native: it translates event contracts into sportsbook mental models (American odds, bet-slip flow, parlay-like combos) rather than teaching users order books and probabilities. Marketing language says "trading," not betting/gaming — a framing choice criticized by NCPG as dodging gambling-harm norms.
visualLanguage: Reviewers consistently describe the app as mirroring the DraftKings Sportsbook aesthetic: dark sportsbook-style layouts, color-coded green (Yes/buy) and red (No) action buttons, and a "Trade Slip" panel that "visually mimics a sportsbook bet slip." Sports markets are rendered in a moneyline/spread/totals grid — the classic three-column sportsbook game row — with American odds as the default price representation; the Yes/No binary card treatment only surfaces prominently in politics, crypto, and economics categories. Notably ABSENT from the visual system (per BettingUSA): price-history charts, order-book/depth displays, and volume stats — i.e., none of the financial-terminal visual furniture Kalshi/Polymarket use. The product communicates probability through odds numbers, not through graphs. Quick-add stake chips (+$5, +$10, +$20) are described as "directly imported from the DraftKings Sportsbook."
typographyBrand: No direct on-site observation possible (site blocked; see evidenceNotes), so this is the weakest-evidence section. Inference from multiple reviewer statements that the app "mirrors DraftKings Sportsbook's aesthetic": DK's established brand system — black/dark surfaces, signature DraftKings green as the primary action color, condensed geometric sans headline type with high-density numeric tables — is carried over rather than a new financial-brand identity being created. The brand name itself does the trust work ("DraftKings" + "Predictions"), and the App Store listing leads with the parent brand. Assumption: exact typefaces unverified. The June 2026 DKeX move folds prediction markets INTO the flagship "DraftKings: Sports and Casino" app brand rather than building the standalone Predictions brand further — a signal that DK treats predictions as a product line, not a distinct brand.
navigationDiscovery: Desktop web (per WSN, July 2026): sports-first layout with league sections (NBA, MLB, Tennis, PGA) directly in the main navigation bar; within a league, markets are grouped into sportsbook-style buckets — e.g., NBA playoffs split into "Games, Series Winners, Correct Score, and Futures." Non-sports discovery is by category tabs: Economics (Fed funds rate, NFP, unemployment, GDP, CPI), Stock Market (CME E-mini S&P 500 strike/intraday-window contracts), Commodities, Crypto (daily BTC/ETH price markets), Politics (Congress, governors, presidential), Business, and Entertainment/Culture (added post-launch). There is no search-forward or trending/volume-sorted discovery described anywhere — discovery is taxonomy-driven like a sportsbook lobby, not feed-driven like Polymarket. Reviewers flag shallow depth per category ("NFL markets are largely limited to point spreads, outright winners, and Super Bowl futures" — BettingUSA), so navigation is broad-category shallow-leaf.
marketCardAnatomy: Two card grammars coexist. (1) Sports cards: sportsbook game-row layout showing the matchup with moneyline/spread/totals columns, each cell showing American odds (e.g., +150 / -163) rather than cent prices — tapping a cell adds it to the Trade Slip. (2) Binary event cards (politics/econ/crypto): stated outcome question ("Will the Republican Party win the presidential election in 2028?") with green Yes / red No buttons, American odds rendered alongside the $0.01–$0.99 contract price, e.g., an Economics card listing "Cut ≤25bps — Yes +900" (LocalsInsider). Stock-market cards show strike prices across multiple intraday windows. What cards do NOT carry (per BettingUSA): volume, liquidity/depth, price-history sparkline, or trader counts. Settlement-rule access is per-market via predefined rules specifying the grading method and official data source, but reviewers place fee/payout detail behind an info icon in the ticket rather than on the card face.
tradeTicketClarity: The strongest-documented surface. The "Trade Slip" works like a bet slip: user enters a DOLLAR amount (not a contract count); the platform auto-calculates the number of shares purchasable plus applicable fees, and shows projected total payout in sportsbook terms (e.g., "$238 total on $100 at +150"). Quick-add chips (+$5/+$10/+$20). An information icon "opens a detailed payout breakdown that clearly explains fees, share pricing, and projected returns" (WSN); TheLines confirms "fee structure at checkout, so you know the charges that apply." Rough edges: dollar-to-shares conversion leaves unspent residue (a $10 entry may fill only $9.96); market orders only, no limit orders; and the per-CONTRACT fee (~$0.02/contract/side, i.e., $0.01 DK + $0.01 exchange per ValueTheMarkets; WSN reports $0.01 at extreme prices $0.01–$0.19 and $0.97–$0.99) means effective fee percentage balloons on longshots — BettingUSA computes a $100 order costing between $2.12 and $25 in fees depending on contract price, which the odds-forward UI does not make intuitive. Distinctive feature: "Combos" — up to 6 event contracts combined into a single trade where every leg must win (a parlay transplanted into a prediction market).
trustRiskSafety: Regulatory trust is front-loaded: App Store description states "GUS III LLC d/b/a DraftKings Predictions is a CFTC-registered Introducing Broker" and "Trading involves substantial risk of loss and is not suitable for everyone"; 18+ age rating with in-app age-assurance controls. Fees: ~$0.02 per contract per side ($0.01 DK + $0.01 exchange per ValueTheMarkets; WSN reports $0.01 at price extremes), disclosed at checkout behind the ticket's info icon rather than on market cards; no deposit/withdrawal/inactivity fees; $5 min deposit, $1 min withdrawal; ACH withdrawals 2–7 business days; funds custodied at Wedbush Securities (broker-dealer). Resolution: contracts settle automatically at $1.00/$0.00 per predefined per-market settlement rules that specify grading method and the official data source; users can sell out before resolution. Responsible-use surface: a "Responsible Trading" area with daily/weekly/monthly deposit limits, limit history, cool-off periods, self-exclusion (long-term or permanent), plus a "smart trading guide" resource. Documented gaps (Sportico Jan 9, 2026; NCPG): at launch no gambling-addiction hotline info, no session-time tracking, no betting-history visualizations; 18+ threshold vs 21+ on DK's own sportsbook; Predictions wallet is siloed from the sportsbook and sources describe no cross-product self-exclusion linkage. Sector context: 11 states have issued cease-and-desist orders against prediction-market operators as unlicensed sports betting (MultiState, Mar 19, 2026), and NCPG publicly urged operators to adopt sportsbook-grade safeguards.
socialCommunity: Effectively none. BettingUSA explicitly lists "social features" among missing capabilities alongside order books and price history, saying the product feels "more like a beta testing platform than a finished product"; TheLines' walkthrough describes no comments, profiles, leaderboards, follower graphs, or market-level discussion — a sharp contrast with Polymarket's comment threads and holder lists. DraftKings' community strategy appears to be external (its existing sportsbook CRM, promos like a "100% match on your first trade up to $75 in Prediction Dollars," and cross-sell into the unified DraftKings app) rather than in-product social. Support is transactional: 24/7 chatbot, ticket submission, and callback requests plus a self-service help center covering deposits, settlement, and verification.
mobileUsability: Mobile-first by design and well-received: standalone iOS app rated 4.8/5 (~3.7K ratings, "Sports" category, 18+), Android ~4.4/5; bi-weekly release cadence (v1.11.0 on June 30, 2026). The sportsbook interaction grammar — tap an odds cell, slip slides up, dollar-entry keypad with quick-add chips, single confirm — is inherently thumb-optimized and requires no trading knowledge; reviewers repeatedly note sportsbook users need no tutorial. Onboarding is standard gambling-app KYC compressed to mobile: email → username/password → phone → DOB/address → SSN last-4 + government ID → geolocation check → $5+ deposit; existing DraftKings credentials log in directly (shared identity) but the wallet is separate from sportsbook funds. Post-June 2026, DKeX prediction markets also surface inside the unified "DraftKings: Sports and Casino" app, including live in-play contracts — meaning predictions inherit that app's mature mobile infrastructure. Weaknesses on mobile: no charts or portfolio analytics, market-order-only execution, and fee math hidden one tap deep.
learnFrom: Translate contracts into the user's native mental model: sports rows use moneyline/spread/totals with American odds, and Yes/No only appears where no betting idiom exists — meet users where their intuition already is instead of teaching order books.
Dollar-first ticket entry: user types what they want to risk; the system computes share count, fees, and projected payout — quantity-of-contracts is an implementation detail, not a user decision.
Quick-add stake chips (+$5/+$10/+$20) reduce keypad friction on mobile and anchor small stakes.
One tap from ticket to full cost transparency: the info-icon payout breakdown (fees + share price + projected return) is a good pattern — cost math on demand without cluttering the happy path.
Shared identity, separate wallet: letting existing account credentials work while ring-fencing funds lowered onboarding friction without commingling regulatory regimes.
Predefined per-market settlement rules naming the official data source, with automatic $1/$0 settlement — resolution certainty as a product feature.

Responsible-use toolkit shipped day one (daily/weekly/monthly deposit limits, limit history, cool-off, permanent self-exclusion) and named neutrally ('Responsible Trading') to fit the product's framing.

Own the venue over time: launch on someone else's rails (IB → CME) to ship fast, then vertically integrate (Railbird → DKeX) to remove per-trade exchange fees and control listing speed — a sequencing lesson for any market operator.
Combos (multi-leg contract bundles) as an engagement/monetization mechanic imported from parlays — high-margin, high-excitement, and unique among prediction markets.
Category-first lobby navigation (league sections, market-type groupings) makes a shallow catalog feel organized rather than empty.
avoid: Per-contract flat fees hidden behind an odds-forward UI: a $100 longshot order can cost up to ~$25 in fees while a favorite costs ~$2 — fee-as-%-of-stake is invisible when users think in dollars and odds. Show effective fee percentage on the ticket face.

Stripping out ALL market microstructure (no price history, no volume, no depth, no limit orders): it lowers the floor but caps the ceiling — power users churn to Kalshi/Polymarket, and reviewers read the absence as 'beta product.' Offer a progressive-disclosure advanced view instead.
Dollar-entry residue ($10 in, $9.96 filled, $0.04 stranded) with no explanation — either round transparently or auto-handle remainders.

Framing-driven safety gaps: calling it 'trading' while omitting problem-gambling hotlines, session-time data, and history visualizations invited NCPG/press attacks on hypocrisy. If the product is functionally wagering, ship wagering-grade safeguards regardless of the legal wrapper.
Siloed self-exclusion: an 18+ product that a 21+ sportsbook self-excluded user can apparently still access is a reputational landmine — safety states should follow the person, not the product line.
Zero community/social layer in a category where conviction and discussion drive liquidity — no comments, leaderboards, or trader signal leaves engagement entirely dependent on promos and CRM.
Broad-category, shallow-leaf catalogs: launching whole categories (politics, crypto) with only a handful of thin markets each makes the lobby feel emptier than fewer, deeper categories would.

Regulatory-arbitrage positioning without a communications plan: entering states as 'not gambling' triggered cease-and-desist campaigns and a $600M-tax-revenue narrative against the sector — anticipate and pre-answer the 'you're just unlicensed betting' attack.

Non-withdrawable bonus currencies ('Prediction Dollars') with expiry/trading restrictions read as sportsbook promo mechanics and invite mistrust in a product asking to be treated as a financial venue.
evidenceNotes: DIRECT EVIDENCE LIMITATION: predictions.draftkings.com (root and /en/how-to-trade-predictions-availability) returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, and the sandboxed browser pane blocked the origin by policy, so I made NO first-hand observation of the live product UI; per instructions I did not fabricate on-site details. DIRECT EVIDENCE (fetched full pages): Apple App Store listing (developer, 4.8/3.7K rating, 18+, GUS III LLC IB language, v1.11.0 Jun 30 2026, risk disclaimer); Sportico RG article (NCPG quotes, missing-safeguard list, DK spokesperson tool list); BettorsInsider DKeX launch article (Jun 26 2026 launch, unified-app integration, $11.3B/$3.4B volume, fee-elimination rationale, Robins quote); ValueTheMarkets (IB→CME routing, Wedbush custody, fee decomposition, CFTC rule-withdrawal claim); BettingUSA, WSN, TheLines, LocalsInsider, BettorsInsider reviews (all UI descriptions — nav, cards, Trade Slip, quick-add chips, green/red buttons, combo feature, fee tiers, onboarding steps, RG tools). These reviewer UI descriptions are SECONDARY evidence — consistent across 4+ independent outlets, so I treat convergent details (bet-slip ticket, dollar entry, American odds default, missing charts/order book/social) as reliable; single-source details (fee tier at price extremes [WSN], $9.96 residue example [WSN], Venmo/PayPal deposits [TheLines], Wedbush custody [VTM]) are flagged to one source. INFERENCE: fee reconciliation (~$0.02/contract/side total, cheaper at extremes) synthesized from three partially conflicting accounts; 'taxonomy-driven, no trending/search discovery' inferred from absence across all walkthroughs; sportsbook self-exclusion silo inferred from separate-wallet + separate-app structure and Sportico criticism, not from an explicit statement. ASSUMPTION: typography specifics (typefaces, exact palette values) assumed to carry over from DraftKings' sportsbook brand based on reviewers' 'mirrors sportsbook aesthetic' language — unverified. DISCARDED: predictionmarketspicks.com page contained apparent errors (claimed DK operates under state sportsbook licenses, not CFTC; nav items like '7 Oracles' appear to be the review site's own chrome) and was excluded. State-availability counts conflict across sources (38 vs 40+ vs 48 states; sports contracts in 14–18 states) — reported as ranges; the discrepancy likely reflects expansion between Dec 2025 and Jul 2026 snapshots. Volume figures ($11.3B annualized) are DraftKings' own claims, not independently verified.
